track.name: restructuring
track.label: Distressed Debt & Restructuring
track.summary: The technical core of restructuring and turnaround advisory — 13-week cash flow modeling, distressed valuation, the Chapter 11 process, and how to actually break into firms like Alvarez & Marsal and FTI Consulting.

phases.title: Foundations of Corporate Distress & the Restructuring Industry
phases.description: Understand why companies actually fail, map the firms and roles that make up the restructuring industry, and learn the real, documented paths students use to break in.

phases.title: The Legal & Process Framework
phases.description: Learn the mechanics of Chapter 11, Chapter 7, and out-of-court workouts — DIP financing, creditor committees, claims administration, and how priority of claims determines who gets paid.

phases.title: 13-Week Cash Flow Modeling
phases.description: Master the single technical skill A&M and FTI both name explicitly in recruiting — building, stress-testing, and presenting a 13-week cash flow model that lenders and creditors actually trust.

phases.title: Distressed Valuation & Credit Analysis
phases.description: Value a distressed company under liquidation and going-concern scenarios, map the capital structure to find the fulcrum security, and build a recovery waterfall.

phases.title: Turnaround & Operational Restructuring
phases.description: Diagnose the operating business behind the balance sheet — build an EBITDA bridge, structure a long-term business plan, and study how real companies turned around or didn't.

phases.title: Breaking In & Client-Facing Craft
phases.description: Prepare for the unusually technical restructuring interview, position a non-traditional background convincingly, and understand where CIRA, CTP, and CFA fit in a restructuring career.

topics.title: Why Companies Fail — Liquidity, Solvency & the Distress Cycle
topics.description: Distinguish a liquidity problem from a solvency problem, learn the early warning signs of financial distress, and understand the cycle that pulls a company from underperformance toward restructuring.

steps.d: Define liquidity problems (cannot meet short-term obligations) vs. solvency problems (liabilities exceed assets) by working through a company balance sheet showing negative equity but positive cash flow.

steps.t: Map warning signs in financial statements
steps.d: List the eight early warning signs of distress — declining EBITDA, covenant violations, excessive debt, falling liquidity, rising burn rate — and identify each one in real quarterly filings.
Diagram how underperformance triggers covenant breach, which triggers lender pressure, which forces asset sales, which accelerates decline, using a specific timeline (6-18 months pre-filing).

steps.t: Measure the point of no return
steps.d: Calculate the exact moment a company's cash runway expires by projecting weekly cash burn and identifying the week it hits zero without a restructuring or financing event.

Reread your liquidity vs. solvency conclusion and verify you could explain to a lender why the company chose restructuring over these alternatives: asset sale, dividend suspension, or debt covenant waiver.

topics.title: The Restructuring Industry Landscape — Consulting Firms, RX Banks & Law Firms
topics.description: Map the players — turnaround consultancies like A&M and FTI, restructuring investment banks like PJT and Houlihan Lokey, and the law firms that run the courtroom side of a case.

steps.t: Map the big three consulting firms
steps.d: List the 'big three' turnaround consultancies — Alvarez & Marsal, FTI Consulting, Lazard — and name the one other firm in their peer tier, then verify by checking recent restructuring case mandates in DebtDomain or case law dockets.

steps.t: Compare RX banking and turnaround consulting
steps.d: Build a two-column table showing how restructuring investment banks (PJT, Houlihan Lokey, Centerview) differ from turnaround consultancies in staffing, exit paths, deal types, and client relationships.
Name the three largest restructuring law practices — Weil, Latham, Kirkland — and note which one leads in debtor representations and which in creditor committee work.

steps.t: Trace a case through the ecosystem
steps.d: Pick one recent major Chapter 11 case (Hertz, Bed Bath & Beyond, or a current one) and identify which consulting firm, bank, law firms, and CRO worked the case.
Explain why Alvarez & Marsal and FTI name the 13-week cash flow model in recruiting materials and why that specific tool matters more to them than it does to restructuring banks.

topics.title: Breaking In — Case Competitions, TMA, and the Audit-to-Restructuring Pipeline
topics.description: Learn the real, recurring paths into the industry: the Big 4 audit/valuation/FDD-to-restructuring pipeline, TMA and TMA NextGen as a genuine student differentiator, and named case competitions that award real interviews.

steps.d: Choose one of the three paths — Big 4 audit/FDD-to-restructuring, TMA NextGen, or case competitions — and list the specific roles, timelines, and exit criteria that make it a credible entry point.
Find the National Restructuring Case Competition or Pari Passu Restructuring Case Competition in your region or online, note the case release date and competition schedule, and mark your calendar.
Research promotion timelines at one Big 4 firm (EY, Deloitte, KPMG, or PwC) and identify the typical year to transition from audit or valuation into transaction services restructuring.
Search the Turnaround Management Association's TMA NextGen network and find which law firms, consultancies, and banks in your city have active TMA NextGen programs.

steps.t: Validate entry criteria against your story
steps.d: Write a one-paragraph description of your path into restructuring (which pipeline, what timeline, what you will do in the next 12 months) and reread it against the documented entry patterns in the resources.

topics.title: Chapter 11 vs. Chapter 7 vs. Out-of-Court Workouts
topics.description: Compare reorganization under Chapter 11, liquidation under Chapter 7, and negotiated out-of-court workouts — and understand why a company and its advisors choose one path over another.

topics.title: DIP Financing, Creditor Committees & Claims Administration
topics.description: Learn how debtor-in-possession financing keeps a bankrupt company running, how the official creditors' committee operates, and how proofs of claim and bar dates administer who gets to be paid.

steps.d: List the six stages a DIP financing goes through: need, lender agreement, bankruptcy filing, first-day hearing approval, funding, and covenant oversight — then add the typical timeline (filing to first-day approval in 24-48 hours).

steps.t: Identify covenant mechanics in DIP docs
steps.d: Read a real DIP agreement (from an A&M or Kirkland resource) and extract three budget covenants and three milestone requirements that give the lender monthly control over the debtor's operations.

steps.t: Review a committee objection to DIP fees
steps.d: Find a motion objecting to DIP lender fees in a major Chapter 11 case and identify the categories of UCC objections raised.

Map the claims process from filing (bar date set, typically 70 days post-petition) through creditor proof of claim submission, trustee or debtor objection, and final claims allowance that determines who votes on a plan.

steps.t: Compare your DIP model to reality
steps.d: Draw a one-page diagram of your understanding of how DIP mechanics, creditor committees, and claims administration interact, then validate each element against the U.S. Courts or CFI resources.

topics.title: Absolute Priority, Cramdown & a Brief Look at UK Administration/CVA
topics.description: Understand the absolute priority rule and how a plan gets 'crammed down' over an objecting class, then contrast the US process with UK administration and Company Voluntary Arrangements.

steps.d: Write out the rule in one sentence: Senior claims get paid in full before junior claims receive anything, and name the statutory section that governs it (11 USC 1129(b)).

steps.t: Apply Section 1129(b) to a dissenting class
steps.d: Given a plan where unsecured creditors vote no, verify whether the plan can be confirmed if at least one impaired class votes yes and absolute priority is satisfied.

Using a $100M company with $60M senior debt, $30M unsecured, and $10M equity, walk through enterprise value at five recovery levels (0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 100%) and show who gets paid at each recovery point.

Read the PwC UK articles and write a two-paragraph comparison: (1) how UK Administration differs from Chapter 7, and (2) how UK CVAs differ from Chapter 11 plans — noting that administration is faster and less formal.

steps.t: Apply priority logic to a plan
steps.d: Given a proposed plan in a recent case filing (from a resource), verify that it respects absolute priority by checking whether lower-priority claims receive more than higher-priority claims could have received.

topics.title: Building a 13-Week Cash Flow Model From Scratch
topics.description: Build a direct-method, weekly cash flow model from receipts and disbursements — the exact tool A&M and FTI use as the entry point to almost every restructuring engagement.

steps.d: In a new Excel workbook, create line items for weekly cash receipts (product sales, collections, other) and disbursements (payroll, cost of goods sold, rent, utilities, debt service, capex), using a real company's P&L and balance sheet.

Add rows to show cash tied up in receivables, inventory, and payables, then calculate the weekly cash impact of changes in each (e.g., a $5M accounts receivable buildup reduces cash despite positive revenue).
Check that opening cash plus net weekly cash flow equals closing cash, and that total 13-week net cash flow reconciles to the company's actual month-end cash position in the latest balance sheet.
Build two columns: base case (current collection period, sales trends) and downside (7 days slower collections, 15% volume decline), then show how each scenario changes the cash position by week 13.

steps.t: Present findings to an internal audience
steps.d: Write a one-page memo explaining your model's most critical line items (the ones that swing cash the most) and list the three assumptions you would defend first if a CFO challenged your forecast.

topics.title: Minimum Cash, Liquidity Bridges & Variance Analysis
topics.description: Set a defensible minimum cash threshold, build a liquidity bridge that ties covenant headroom to the forecast, and run the weekly actual-vs-forecast variance process that keeps the model credible.

steps.d: Calculate a defensible minimum cash balance for a specific company by adding: (1) three days of average disbursements, (2) a covenant compliance cushion, and (3) a working capital buffer — then justify this number to a lender in writing.

Create a table showing how the company's leverage ratio, interest coverage ratio, or liquidity covenant headroom changes week by week under your base case, and the exact week where headroom breaks if there is no adjustment.

Pull the company's actual cash position from the prior week's bank statement, compare it to your model forecast, calculate the variance and its causes (sales miss, payment timing, working capital shift), and adjust forward weeks by the same driver.

When you update the model after the first week of actuals, create a table showing which assumptions changed (collection period, disbursement timing, sales trajectory), the magnitude of each change, and the cumulative 13-week impact.

Rerun the variance process for three consecutive weeks and confirm that week-by-week forecast accuracy (actual vs. forecast in week N) is improving as you incorporate actual data and refine assumptions.

topics.title: Stress-Testing and Presenting a 13-Week Cash Flow to Lenders
topics.description: Build base, downside, and stress scenarios into the model, then present it to a skeptical lender group who will challenge every assumption behind it.

steps.d: Create a downside case where collections slow by 10%, sales volume drops 20%, and key supplier terms tighten, then calculate the weekly cash impact and identify the latest week the company can weather this stress without new capital.

Build an even more severe scenario where the downside continues and two key customers default, then determine whether the company would need DIP financing or emergency asset sales to survive 13 weeks.

Build a dashboard with base, downside, and stress columns showing opening cash, weekly net cash flow, and closing cash for week 13, then add a line for 'days of liquidity remaining' to make the stakes clear.
List the five most aggressive assumptions in your stress case (the ones most likely to trigger lender objection) and write one sentence explaining why each one is justified or conservative.

Deliver a five-minute verbal walk-through of your base case to a colleague playing the role of a lender, focusing on the cash position and minimum cash levels, then record how many assumptions the lender questions and whether you can defend each one.

topics.title: Liquidation Value vs. Going-Concern Value
topics.description: Learn the liquidation analysis that sets the 'floor' recovery for creditors, and understand when a business is worth more sold whole and operating than broken apart.

steps.t: Estimate liquidation recovery per asset class
steps.d: Using a real company's balance sheet, estimate forced-sale values for inventory (30-50% of book), receivables (70% assuming some uncollectible), equipment (20-40% of depreciated value), and real estate (80% of appraised value).

Sum the liquidation recoveries less wind-down costs (professional fees, auction expenses, working capital payoff) and express as a percentage of enterprise value to find the minimum recovery creditors can expect.

Build a simplified three-year DCF for the same company assuming it remains operating (stable EBITDA, normalized capex), then compare the DCF value to your liquidation floor to see if going concern creates more value.
Calculate the EBITDA level at which going-concern value equals liquidation value — that is, the level below which the company is worth more liquidated than reorganized.

steps.t: Validate your choice against market evidence
steps.d: Take your going-concern DCF and check whether the implicit EBITDA margin, growth rate, and exit multiple are consistent with comparable company trading multiples or recent transaction multiples in that industry.

topics.title: Capital Structure, Debt Tranches & the Fulcrum Security
topics.description: Map a distressed company's capital stack from senior secured debt down to equity, and identify the fulcrum security — the tranche where enterprise value runs out and control converts to equity.

topics.title: Recovery Analysis & the Distribution Waterfall
topics.description: Build a recovery waterfall that ranks every class of claim by priority and pays them out until enterprise value is exhausted — the core output of any distressed valuation exercise.

steps.d: Using a company with $150M enterprise value, $80M senior debt, $50M unsecured debt, and $20M equity, rank each class by priority and distribute value layer-by-layer, showing exactly who gets paid at each step.
For each class in your waterfall, calculate the recovery percentage (actual value received ÷ stated claim) and express as a cents-on-dollar recovery figure.

steps.t: Show the impact of valuation changes
steps.d: Recalculate your waterfall at two lower enterprise value levels ($120M, $100M) and show how each class's recovery changes, demonstrating which classes are most sensitive to valuation assumptions.

Build three waterfalls for the same company under three scenarios (base, downside, recovery), then summarize the recovery percentage for each class across all three scenarios to show the range of outcomes.

steps.t: Validate your waterfall against a real case
steps.d: Find a confirmed Chapter 11 plan in an actual case filing and extract the distribution waterfall from the plan of reorganization, then verify that your understanding of priority and recovery matches the filed plan.

topics.title: Diagnosing the Business — Cost Structure & EBITDA Bridge Analysis
topics.description: Break a company's cost base down into its real drivers and build an EBITDA bridge that explains, bar by bar, exactly what moved profitability between two periods.

steps.d: Take a company's cost of goods sold and operating expenses and divide them into fixed costs (rent, insurance, corporate overhead) and variable costs (materials, commissions), then calculate the fixed/variable ratio.

Create a waterfall showing period 1 EBITDA, then adding or subtracting each line-item cost change (higher material costs, lower labor, reduced overhead), to arrive at period 2 EBITDA, then repeat this for a second period.

For each bar in your EBITDA bridge, write one sentence explaining the root cause: volume decline, pricing pressure, supply cost inflation, or efficiency improvement — and rank the top three drivers by impact.

Examine your EBITDA bridge and identify costs that are sticky (hard to cut quickly): are fixed costs too high? Are there one-time charges inflating the cost base? What percentage of costs are within management's control in the next 12 months?

Propose what normalized EBITDA would be if the company eliminated structural inefficiencies (excess overhead, underutilized assets, unprofitable product lines) and show the gap between current EBITDA and normalized EBITDA.

topics.title: Building the Long-Term Business Plan
topics.description: Translate the diagnostic and the 13-week forecast into a multi-year business plan that underpins valuation, lender negotiations, and the plan of reorganization itself.

steps.t: Translate the 13-week forecast into a long-term plan
steps.d: Take your 13-week cash flow model, extend it to 52 weeks assuming your downside scenario stabilizes, then project revenue, EBITDA, and cash flow for years 2-3 using industry growth assumptions.

Identify the three specific actions that will drive revenue back to pre-distress levels: new customer wins, price increases, cost reductions driving market share gain — and assign a timeline and probability to each.

Using a normalized EBITDA projection from year 3, apply an industry-appropriate exit multiple (e.g., 6-8x EBITDA for your industry) to calculate the expected enterprise value at plan exit, then show what that means for creditor recoveries.

Translate your year-2 and year-3 projections into quarterly covenant metrics (leverage ratio, interest coverage, liquidity threshold) and demonstrate that the company will emerge from Chapter 11 and immediately comply with exit financing.
Recalculate your long-term plan under a downside scenario (revenue recovery is slower, exit multiple is lower) and show whether creditors still recover adequately and the company is still viable.

topics.title: Case Studies in Real-World Corporate Turnarounds
topics.description: Study well-documented turnarounds and liquidations — American Airlines, Hertz, and Toys 'R' Us among them — to see how the tools in this course played out in practice.

steps.d: Using the CNN Money article and additional research, write a timeline of American Airlines' 2011-2013 Chapter 11: what triggered the filing, what was the business model problem, how did restructuring fix it, and when did it emerge.

Read the FTI case study on Hertz and identify: what business model problem made Hertz structurally challenged, why did COVID accelerate the decline, and what market conditions made Chapter 7 inevitable.

steps.t: Map Toys R Us value destruction
steps.d: Watch the Wall Street Journal video and identify: the leverage added at acquisition, which cost pressures (e-commerce, labor) were structural vs. cyclical, and why LBO leverage combined with retail disruption caused a liquidation.

Pick two of the three cases and write two paragraphs comparing: (1) what would have needed to be true for each company to have restructured and emerged (different capital structure, different markets), and (2) why the actual path was inevitable.
From the three cases, write four statements about what predicts whether a company turns around, gets refinanced, or liquidates.

topics.title: The Restructuring Interview — Technical Case Prep
topics.description: Prepare for an interview process that is unusually technical and light on behavioral questions — candidates report Excel tests and simplified cash-flow model walkthroughs, not case-study frameworks.

steps.d: Work through a simplified 13-week cash flow build from a case interview guide (Wall Street Prep or Hacking the Case Interview), making assumptions about collections, disbursements, and working capital, and calculate minimum cash needed.
Given a capital structure and enterprise value range, build and explain a recovery waterfall, calculating cents-on-dollar recoveries for each class, as if presenting to an interview panel.
Read through a simplified DIP agreement excerpt and identify three key covenants, two exceptions or carve-outs the debtor negotiated, and one place where the lender has disproportionate leverage.

Conduct a mock interview where you present a simplified restructuring model and a colleague acting as an aggressive lender questions your top three assumptions — practice defending each one in 30 seconds.

After completing the above, write a one-paragraph assessment of your weakest technical area (cash flow modeling, valuation, case law, or documentation), then identify one specific practice exercise to close the gap before your real interview.

topics.title: Positioning Your Story — From Audit/Finance Background to Restructuring
topics.description: Turn a Big 4 audit, FDD, or valuation background into a convincing restructuring narrative — what transfers directly, what you need to backfill, and how to frame the pivot.

steps.d: List your Big 4 skills and map each to a restructuring task: analysis to DIP review, modeling to waterfall building, process to case management.

Against the restructuring skill list (chapter law, turnaround strategy, case management, lender management), identify three topics outside your Big 4 experience and commit to learning one deeply before your interview.

Compose a three-sentence elevator pitch: 'In Big 4 role, I did X. That taught me Y. Now I want to do Z in restructuring because restructuring is Y on steroids.' Then test it on a mentor in the industry.
Using LinkedIn or FTI/A&M career pages, find two alumni who transitioned from Big 4 FDD to restructuring consulting, read their profiles for timing and roles, and note commonalities in their paths.

Anticipate a recruiter asking 'Why not stay in FDD or move to corporate finance?' and draft a response that credibly differentiates restructuring (higher stakes, asymmetric returns, deal management) from your previous work.

topics.title: Certifications & Career Pathway — CIRA, CTP, CFA
topics.description: Understand CIRA, CTP, and the CFA charter as career-progression credentials you pursue once you're in the industry, not requirements to break in.

steps.d: From the AIRA website, list the prerequisites for CIRA (years of experience, coursework, exam), note that CIRA is available immediately upon entering the industry, and confirm you can pursue it in year 1-2 post-hiring.
From the TMA website, confirm the CTP requires 3-5 years of insolvency experience, making it a mid-career credential, and note that TMA membership itself is optional for practitioners.

steps.t: Compare CFA value against CIRA and CTP
steps.d: Research whether major restructuring firms (A&M, FTI) list CFA as preferred or required compared to CIRA, and explain why CIRA matters more in the field.
Given your likely hiring timeline and role, decide which if any credentials you should pursue in your first two years, noting that employer sponsorship often covers exam and study costs.

steps.t: Validate that credentials are not requirements
steps.d: Reread the brief course description and confirm that CIRA, CTP, and CFA are described as credentials you pursue in the industry, not barriers to breaking in, and that you should never list missing credentials as a reason you cannot apply to a firm.
